slides.page_title: Why Cache Exists: Locality and the Latency Gap

items: Small, fast store holding a copy of data.
Authoritative home lives elsewhere: DB, disk, remote service.
Also caches computed results, not just fetched rows.
Copy is always allowed to be wrong or absent.
Cross-region RTT: 50-150 ms. Physics, not tuning.
Jumping one layer down buys 10x-1000x.
Temporal: key read now is likely read again soon.
Spatial: nearby keys get read together.
No locality, no cache. Random access defeats every policy.
Zipf: rate of rank-k item ∝ 1/k^s.
Top 1% of keys often serve 50%+ of requests.
So a tiny cache can win a large hit rate.

lines: h=0.95 -> 5% reaches DB   # half the load

blocks.title: 90 to 95 Is Not 5% Better
blocks.text: Backend load is (1-h). Going 90%→95% halves origin QPS. Read the miss side, not the hit side.

items: Cache only helps the fraction of time spent on cached work.
5 ms DB call inside a 500 ms request: caching is noise.
Profile first, then pick what to cache.
A cache can win latency and still let the DB melt.
State the goal before choosing the layer.

slides.page_title: Why Cache Exists: Locality and the Latency Gap (cont.)

items: Working set = keys actively used in a time window.
Cache < working set: thrash, evictions eat the hot set.
Cache >> working set: paying RAM for nothing.
Read/write ratio is the single best screening signal.
Every cache bets data is read more often than changed.
Skip: write-heavy, always-unique, strict-freshness data.
Bank balance mid-transfer, one-time tokens, unique queries.

blocks.title: Vocab Bank
items: hit / miss — was the copy there?
eviction (space) vs expiration (time)
invalidation — truth changed, kill the copy
staleness, coherence, warm vs cold
GET key from cache. On hit, return.
On miss: read DB, SET key with TTL, return.
Cache never talks to the DB itself.

lines: cache.set(k, v, ttl=300) # always a TTL
db.write(k, v)   # source of truth first

items: Updating writes a value that may never be read.
Two concurrent writers can interleave: lost update.
Delete is idempotent and order-tolerant.
Only requested keys land in cache: memory follows demand.
Cache node dies? Misses just fall through to the DB.
Cache a joined DTO, not a row: models can differ.
Every first read is a miss: 3 trips on the cold path.
Cold start after a flush hammers the DB.
Consistency logic duplicated at every call site.

blocks.title: Killing That Race
items: Short TTL: bounds the damage window.
Versioned keys: v1 writes to a dead key.
Delayed dual delete after the write.
CAS or SET NX so the loser cannot clobber.
Prewarm known-hot keys on deploy, before traffic shifts.
Stagger TTLs so a bulk load never expires together.
Cap concurrent DB loads while the cache fills.
Read-through needs a loader fn: Guava CacheLoader, LoadingCache.
Same read semantics, different owner of the fetch.

blocks.title: Default Pick
blocks.text: Cache-aside is the default for web systems: simplest to reason about, degrades gracefully on cache loss, works with any store.

blocks.title: Cache the Miss Too
blocks.text: If a key legitimately does not exist, store a null tombstone with a short TTL. Otherwise the miss path repeats on every single request — that is cache penetration.

items: App writes cache; cache writes DB synchronously; then ack.
Cached keys are always consistent with the DB.
Every write pays cache latency plus DB latency.
Keys written but never read waste space — pair with a TTL.
Write lands in cache, ack immediately.
DB updated asynchronously, usually batched.
Coalesces repeat writes to one key into one DB write.
Huge for counters, view counts, last-seen timestamps.

blocks.title: The Price of Write-Back
items: Node dies with dirty entries: that data is gone.
Needs replication or an append-only WAL.
Or admit out loud: this data is not durable.
Write-back marks modified entries dirty.
Evicting a dirty entry must flush to the store first.
So eviction becomes a write path, with write latency.
Writes go straight to the DB, bypassing the cache.
Typically invalidates the key on the way past.
Fits write-heavy data that is rarely re-read.
Cost: the key just written is a guaranteed next-read miss.

blocks.title: Read-Your-Own-Writes Breaks
blocks.text: Write-around means a user who just saved a profile reads a miss — and worse, a stale value if a replica answers the reload.

items: Cache-aside reads + write-around/invalidate writes: the web default.
Write-through + read-through: the in-library/embedded default.
Mixing per key-family is normal, not a smell.

lines: # reversed: a reader repopulates old v
# before the commit lands. Stale until TTL.

items: Second delete removes anything a concurrent reader wrote.
Tune the delay above replica lag, not below it.
Max age after which an entry is treated as invalid.
Bounds staleness even when invalidation logic is buggy.
Missed an event? TTL still cleans up eventually.
Sliding keeps hot keys alive under steady traffic.
Sliding on a mutable value can pin a wrong copy forever.
Ask: how out-of-date before a user notices or a rule breaks?
That answer is the TTL. Not a round number you liked.
Lazy/passive: checked on read, expired then.
Active: background job samples keys and reaps.
Eviction-on-pressure: memory forces the issue.
Redis uses lazy + sampled active: expired keys hold RAM.

blocks.title: Expired Is Not Evicted
blocks.text: Expiration is time-driven and semantic. Eviction is capacity-driven and opportunistic. Both remove entries, for unrelated reasons.

lines: # no jitter: bulk-loaded keys die together
# -> synchronized miss storm on the origin

items: Negative caching: not-found gets a 30-60s TTL.
Refresh-ahead / SWR: return stale now, refresh async.
Hides refresh latency, holds hit rate near 100%.
Cost: one extra interval of staleness.

lines: soft = 300s  # trigger bg refresh, still serve
hard = 600s  # must not be served past this

blocks.title: TTL Discipline
items: Set TTL at write time; never scan and fix later.
No key without a TTL unless explicitly invalidated.
TTL-less keys are the top cause of unbounded growth.

blocks.title: TTL Bounds Damage, Not Truth
blocks.text: A 5-minute TTL does not make you consistent. It means up to 5 minutes of every user seeing a wrong value.

items: Cache is full, a new entry needs space.
Policy picks who dies. That is the whole job.
Bélády optimal: evict the item used furthest in the future.
Unimplementable — needs the future. So all policies guess.

slides.page_title: Eviction Policies I: LRU, LFU, CLOCK

items: Evict the entry untouched longest.
Hash map for lookup + doubly linked list for order.
O(1) get and put; recency is a pointer move.

blocks.title: LRU's Scan Problem
blocks.text: One full table scan or nightly batch touches every key once and pushes the entire hot set out the tail. LRU is not scan-resistant.

items: Evict the lowest access count.
Better than LRU on stable, skewed workloads.
Pollution: yesterday's viral key keeps a huge count forever.
Fix with aging — halve counters periodically — or a window.
allkeys-lru and allkeys-lfu sample N random keys.
maxmemory-samples default 5, not a global list.
Near-LRU quality at a fraction of the bookkeeping.
8-bit logarithmic counter, incremented probabilistically.
Plus a decay time so old heat drains away.
Fits inside existing object metadata: no extra structure.
FIFO evicts the oldest inserted, use ignored. Cheap, weak.
CLOCK: FIFO ring plus one reference bit per entry.
Hand sweeps: bit set → clear and skip; bit clear → evict.
Approximates LRU with no per-access list surgery.
CLOCK is why OS page replacement can be cheap at scale.
Second-chance = CLOCK under its older name.

slides.page_title: Eviction Policies II: TinyLFU and Tuning

items: SLRU splits into probationary and protected segments.
New keys enter probation; a second hit promotes them.
So a one-hit wonder cannot evict a long-lived hot key.
ARC self-tunes the split between recency and frequency.
Small LRU admission window in front of the main cache.
Frequency estimated by a Count-Min Sketch, not real counters.
New key admitted only if its est. frequency beats the victim's.
Caffeine's default: near-optimal hit rate, tiny metadata.
allkeys-random: zero bookkeeping, pick any victim.
Surprisingly acceptable when the hit rate is already very high.
Common fallback under memory pressure.
volatile-lru / -lfu / -ttl / -random: only keys with a TTL.
volatile-ttl prefers the entry closest to expiring.
Keys with no TTL are never candidates.

blocks.title: The volatile-* Trap
blocks.text: A full cache of TTL-less keys under volatile-lru has no legal victim — Redis starts returning OOM errors on every write.

items: Reject writes with an error once maxmemory is hit.
Correct when the store is a queue or a source of truth.
Dangerous when the store is genuinely a cache.
Track evictions/sec, hit rate, memory fragmentation together.
Evictions rising + hit rate falling = undersized for working set.
Evictions rising + hit rate flat = harmless churn on cold keys.

slides.page_title: Eviction Policies II: TinyLFU and Tuning (cont.)

blocks.title: Before Swapping Policy
items: Confirm you are evicting, not expiring.
Check fragmentation: RSS can lie about usable memory.
More RAM often beats a cleverer policy.
Explicit delete on write: prompt, but app must never miss a path.
TTL only: accept bounded staleness, zero coordination.
Event/CDC-driven: subscribe to the change stream and delete.
CDC sources: Debezium, MySQL binlog, transactional outbox.
At-least-once with correct ordering, hundreds of ms lag.
Flat deterministic keys are computable from the write.
Derived/aggregate keys: one write dirties thousands.

lines: # old entry is unreferenced, dies by TTL

items: One write invalidates a whole family of keys.
Standard group-flush trick; old generation ages out.
Attach tags to entries, invalidate by tag.
Fastly surrogate keys, Varnish bans do exactly this.
Cost: maintaining the tag→key index yourself.
In-process caches: every app node holds its own copy.
A delete must be broadcast, or nodes drift apart.
Channels: pub/sub, Redis keyspace notifications, gossip.
Invalidate synchronously before responding to the writer, or
Pin that user to primary / skip cache for a short window.

blocks.title: Not Atomic, Ever
blocks.text: DB write and cache delete are two operations. Crash between them and the cache is stale until TTL — which is exactly why every key still needs a TTL.

items: Flush-all trades correctness for a herd on the origin.
Prefer targeted deletes or generation bumps.

blocks.title: Safest to Riskiest
items: versioned keys > CDC-driven delete
> write-then-delete > write-then-update
> TTL only
Remote also pays serialization on every get and set.
Local pays duplication: N nodes, N copies, N drifts.
L1 local in front of L2 remote.
Best latency with bounded duplication.
Needs an invalidation broadcast to keep L1 honest.
This is where most stale-data bugs actually live.
Keys and nodes map onto a hash ring; key goes clockwise.
Add or remove a node: only ~1/N of keys remap.
Modulo hashing remaps nearly everything — a full cold cache.

caption.text: Most "add a cache" answers stop at Redis — but the interview (and the incident) is decided by what happens when the key expires. 10 pages of handwritten notes: the read/write patterns, TTL mechanics and jitter, how LRU/LFU/W-TinyLFU actually evict, invalidation that survives races, and the failure modes — stampede, penetration, avalanche — with the fix for each. Save it before your next system design round.
